docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: Benchmarking can be viewed as a constrained adjustment of the model estimates so that their population-weighted aggregate reproduces the trusted higher-level total. For poverty rates and mean welfare, the Workbench applies a region-level (or national) ratio adjustment: a common multiplicative factor within each benchmark area, used to keep benchmarked rates non-negative and preserve the proportional ordering of areas. This is an implementation choice, not the only possibility: ratio/raking adjustments, additive or difference benchmarking adjustments, and more general constrained benchmarking schemes are available in the small-area estimation benchmarking literature (Datta et al., 2011; Bell, Datta, and Ghosh, 2013).
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Benchmarking applies a common ratio factor within each national or grouped benchmark area so that the population-weighted aggregate matches the target. A positive factor preserves nonnegativity and ordering only for predictions that are already nonnegative. It does not repair negative predictions or ensure an upper bound of one; check both bounds for poverty estimates. Ratio benchmarking is an implementation choice among alternatives including additive, difference and more general constrained adjustments (Datta et al., 2011; Bell, Datta, and Ghosh, 2013).

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: Within the benchmarking step, if a target or the model aggregate is missing, or the aggregate is close to zero, the factor is set to 1, so the target is not guaranteed to be met. And the ratio does not keep poverty rates at or below 1.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Nonfinite inputs are rejected. A zero model aggregate with a nonzero target cannot satisfy the constraint and is an error. For a zero target and zero model aggregate within numerical tolerance, UFH sets the group predictions to zero and records an undefined ratio; MFH retains them with factor 1. These are explicit degenerate-case conventions. Inspect any recorded unavailable-benchmark status rather than assuming that a unit adjustment was applied. The ratio does not keep poverty rates at or below 1.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: This cross-year dependence has a concrete source. Households in the same primary sampling unit (PSU) share a persistent cluster effect, so whenever a survey reuses the same PSUs across rounds – through rotating panels, retained clusters, or a panel component – the two years’ direct estimates for an area become positively correlated; the covariance is zero when the two waves are drawn independently. A practical consequence is that the covariance should be estimated from the full survey design in both rounds, not only from the re-interviewed (panel) households, because every household in a shared PSU carries the cluster effect; restricting the calculation to the linked households discards most of the covariance and understates it. With the PSUs declared as the first-stage units, an ordinary survey-design covariance command (for example, R’s survey package) estimates this quantity directly and consistently (Yoshida, 2025).
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Under a persistent positive cluster-effect model, reused PSUs can induce positive cross-year covariance even when different households are sampled. Its actual magnitude and sign depend on the joint survey design, population evolution and overlap; PSU reuse alone does not establish either. Estimate covariance using the correctly specified joint design, stable PSU identifiers and the full relevant sample, including non-panel households in shared PSUs. Independent sampling supports zero design covariance. Review design assumptions and sensitivity to the working covariance specification (Yoshida, 2025).

already_applied: The variances entering this formula can be the direct variances (rho_dir); sm_out variances, for which a finite direct variance is retained when it is at least 0.001 and a missing, non-finite, or smaller value is replaced with its GVF-smoothed value (rho_sm_out); or fully smoothed variances (rho_sm_all). The national-correlation options adapt the nationally pooled sampling-correlation strategy of Boonstra and van den Brakel (2019) to PSU-level dependence, for situations in which area-level covariance estimates are too unstable to use directly: the national sampling-error correlation is estimated from the full sample and combined with domain variances on the selected basis. New configurations pair sm_all with rho_sm_all; rho_sm_out remains an optional sensitivity. Annex G.8 describes the calculation, and Annex H explains its relationship to the published framework.

The package offers direct domain covariance, zero covariance, and national-correlation options. The default rho_sm_all combines a national sampling-error correlation with fully smoothed variances; rho_sm_out remains optional with selective smoothing. These options adapt the nationally pooled sampling-correlation strategy of Boonstra and van den Brakel (2019) to PSU-level dependence when domain covariance estimates are unstable. This pooled construction remains an application extension, even though full variance smoothing now follows the paper's illustration more closely.

Responsibility. The core UFH/MFH framework follows Molina and Romero (2025); the national-correlation options, including the rho_sm_all default, adapt the nationally pooled sampling-correlation strategy of Boonstra and van den Brakel (2019) to PSU-level dependence. The package team is responsible for the software integration, safeguards, documentation, and validation of the resulting implementation.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: Why BH differs: when many areas are tested, some small raw p-values will occur by chance. The BH procedure orders all area-level p-values and adjusts them to control the expected false-discovery rate among the changes declared significant, under its assumptions.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Multiplicity. BH controls the expected false-discovery rate under its assumptions; Bonferroni controls familywise error for the declared family of tests. Molina and Romero (2025, p37) accept individual-area comparisons, explain that a family of area tests needs correction such as Bonferroni, and caution against many-area testing because power becomes poor. Neither correction repairs invalid underlying p-values.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: How to read the outputs. p_value and significant_unadjusted are pointwise results. p_value_bh and significant_bh are BH-adjusted results. docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: How to read the outputs. p_value and significant_unadjusted are pointwise results; p_value_bh and significant_bh are BH results; p_value_bonferroni and significant_bonferroni are Bonferroni results. docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: The package intentionally shows both inferential views. Pointwise intervals answer an area-specific question and are appropriate when a particular area was selected independently of its result. BH adjustment addresses the different question created by reviewing many area-level tests together: it controls the expected false-discovery rate among rejected hypotheses, under its assumptions (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). The two classifications can therefore differ without either calculation being wrong.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Pointwise intervals answer an individual-area question when the area was selected independently of its result. BH controls the false-discovery rate under its assumptions (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995); Bonferroni controls familywise error for a declared family. Molina and Romero (2025, p37) explain the family correction and caution that many-area testing has poor power. These inferential questions must remain distinct.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: The primary figures continue to use pointwise significance, consistent with whether each pointwise 95% confidence interval excludes zero. Tables retain p_value_bh and significant_bh so reviewers can assess multiplicity sensitivity. Reports should identify which rule supports the headline conclusion and should not describe a large set of pointwise findings as family-wide evidence. See the interpretation box in Section 8.12.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Primary figures use pointwise significance, consistent with whether a usable pointwise 95% interval excludes zero. Their counts across areas are exploratory. Tables retain p_value_bh/significant_bh and p_value_bonferroni/significant_bonferroni. Identify the inferential family and rule for any familywide conclusion. Neither adjustment repairs boundary-sensitive undercoverage. See Section 8.12 and docs/MOLINA_ROMERO_DEVIATIONS_w5p.md.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: Recommended practice is to use direct variances when they are stable and credible; use sm_out when very small direct variances risk overstating precision; use sm_all when direct variance estimates are broadly unstable; compare results under alternative variance options as a sensitivity check; and document the variance treatment used in the final model. Under the implemented sm_out rule, a finite direct variance is retained when it is at least 0.001, while a missing, non-finite, or smaller value is replaced with its GVF-smoothed value. Large direct variances are not replaced by sm_out.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Start with sm_all, which replaces all working sampling variances with GVF predictions and follows the full-smoothing illustration in Molina and Romero (2025) most closely. Compare with direct when design variances are credible and with sm_out as an optional sensitivity, and document the chosen treatment. Under sm_out, a finite direct variance at least 0.001 is retained; a missing, non-finite, or strictly smaller value is replaced with its GVF prediction. Large direct variances are not replaced. Full smoothing still requires suitable GVF fit and diagnostics.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: Two practical cautions apply. First, the variances used on the diagonal of the covariance matrix and the variances used inside its off-diagonal covariances should share the same basis; the Workbench ties covariance choices to the variance option for this reason. Second, non-zero covariance inputs can make a multivariate fit more difficult. If convergence fails, first verify year and PSU identifiers and inspect the covariance estimates; then consider moving from unstable direct domain covariances to rho_sm_out or another documented stabilized specification. The rho_sm_out option adapts the nationally pooled sampling-correlation strategy of Boonstra and van den Brakel (2019) to PSU-level dependence. Setting covariance to zero should be a last resort unless survey rounds are genuinely independent, because doing so can misstate the uncertainty of changes over time (Yoshida, 2025).
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Two practical cautions apply. First, the variances used on the diagonal of the covariance matrix and the variances used inside its off-diagonal covariances should share the same basis; the Workbench offers compatible covariance choices for this reason. An omitted covariance setting is derived from the effective variance choice (sm_all with rho_sm_all, sm_out with rho_sm_out, direct with rho_dir); explicit saved settings are preserved. Second, non-zero covariance inputs can make a multivariate fit more difficult. If convergence fails, first verify year and PSU identifiers and inspect the covariance estimates; then consider moving from unstable direct domain covariances to rho_sm_all or another documented stabilized specification. The national-correlation approach adapts the nationally pooled sampling-correlation strategy of Boonstra and van den Brakel (2019) to PSU-level dependence. Setting covariance to zero should be a last resort unless survey rounds are genuinely independent, because doing so can misstate the uncertainty of changes over time (Yoshida, 2025).

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: When MFH estimates are produced under the two-year rolling publication policy, state which estimates are provisional or final, archive each release's estimation window and vintage, and record the once-only routine revision. The NSO must enforce freezing and document exceptional reopening. A within-run MSE/MCPE change test does not apply automatically to published estimates retained from different windows.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: Use arcsine with package bias correction for UFH headcounts, BIC for UFH selection, AIC for MFH selection and MFH2 as starting settings; review diagnostics and sensitivity. Log mean-welfare models target arithmetic area means. UFH uses emdi Slud–Maiti correction and MFH uses conditional-lognormal correction. For MFH, sm_out with rho_sm_out is a starting choice when sampling dependence is plausible and Direct covariance estimates are unstable. The 0.001 variance threshold is an application rule, on the modeled response scale. Use zero covariance only for independent rounds or a documented sensitivity. The shared Bootstrap replicates default is 500; inspect Monte Carlo error, convergence and boundary sensitivity.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: A further limitation is specific to annual production. MFH requires at least two years of data, and because it jointly estimates several years, the poverty estimate for any given year depends on the data window used in the model run. The same year can therefore receive a slightly different estimate depending on which years are included. In annual production, this creates a practical revision issue. A 2025 poverty map, for example, may first be produced from a 2024–2025 data window; once 2026 data become available, the 2025 estimate can be updated using a 2025–2026 data window.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: MFH estimates for a given year depend on the data window used to fit the joint model. The two-period implementation supports a manageable official-statistics revision policy: each newly reported year is provisional, is routinely revised once when it becomes the earlier year in the next window, and is then frozen. This operational rationale for T = 2 does not change the general multivariate model in Molina and Romero (2025).

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: Policy 1: finalize the first year of each two-year MFH run. Under this policy, the second-year estimate is published as preliminary and replaced by the first-year estimate from the following run. For example, the 2025 poverty rate from the 2024-2025 run is preliminary. The 2025 rate from the 2025-2026 run becomes final, while the 2026 rate is preliminary. Once finalized, an estimate is retained unless an exceptional data correction or methodological change requires revision.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: Policy 1: finalize the earlier year of each two-year MFH run. For successive windows (2022, 2024), (2024, 2025), and (2025, 2026), publish 2024 provisionally from the first run, revise and finalize it in the second, then retain that frozen 2024 estimate. Publish 2025 provisionally in the second run, revise and finalize it in the third, and publish 2026 provisionally. At each release, at most one previously published year is routinely revised. The initial window need not contain consecutive calendar years; the initial earlier year's publication status requires an NSO decision.

For successive windows (2022, 2024), (2024, 2025), and (2025, 2026), publish 2024 provisionally from the first run, revise and finalize it in the second, then retain that frozen 2024 estimate. Publish 2025 provisionally in the second run, revise and finalize it in the third, and publish 2026 provisionally. At each release, at most one previously published year is routinely revised. The initial window need not contain consecutive calendar years; the initial earlier year's publication status requires an NSO decision.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: Longer windows make this policy harder to manage. If the oldest year is finalized and newer years are published provisionally, a three-year window leaves two preliminary years in each release. The 2024 rate first appears in the 2022-2024 run, is revised in the 2023-2025 run, and becomes final in the 2024-2026 run. Finalization therefore waits for two subsequent years of data, and each annual release updates two previously published preliminary rates. A four-year window increases the delay to three years and updates three preliminary rates. Already-final estimates need not be revised. This increases the revision history that users must understand and the statistical office must maintain.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: With T > 2, a rolling-window policy that finalizes the oldest year can leave several overlapping years provisional. Those years may be revised repeatedly before finalization, increasing publication delays and the revision history to maintain. T = 2 limits that routine revision burden under Policy 1. Window length alone neither freezes past estimates nor prevents reopening them: the NSO must maintain a vintage archive, enforce the agreed freeze, and document exceptional data corrections or methodological revisions.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: The current Package supports two-year MFH runs. The publication policy should be agreed before releasing results. Record the estimation window and retain the uncertainty measures associated with each published estimate. Policy 1 allows subsequent-year information to revise the latest estimate before finalization; Policy 2 provides a final latest-year estimate without routine revision. Longer windows could offer additional borrowing, but under Policy 1 they add delays and provisional revisions, while under Policy 2 more estimates from each run remain outside the published series. Neither policy removes the need for model validation or a coherent uncertainty calculation.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: The Workbench fits exactly two selected years, but it does not enforce adjacency, a rolling release schedule, or a publication freeze. Agree the publication policy before releasing results and archive each published estimate with its window, vintage and uncertainty. Policy 1 uses one subsequent window to revise the latest year before freezing it; Policy 2 publishes the latest year as final without routine revision. Longer windows may offer more borrowing, but can increase overlapping provisional revisions under Policy 1. Neither policy removes model-validation requirements or supplies uncertainty for differences between estimates from different runs.

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: The Workbench operationalizes a two-year comparison window. This is an implementation scope limit, not a different statistical model.
docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.new: The Workbench uses T = 2 to support an official-statistics policy with one routine revision per newly reported year: publish provisionally, revise when it becomes the earlier year in the next window, then freeze. At most one prior year is routinely revised per release. This avoids repeated revisions of several overlapping years possible with longer windows. Freezing, exceptional reopening and the vintage archive remain NSO policy, not automatic consequences of T = 2 (Section 15.2).

docs/guidance/guidelines_v5_2_0_rc6_wiza.old: The multivariate model adds parameters, and estimating them reliably requires a reasonably large number of areas. With too few areas, the estimation can fail to converge or can return inadmissible values, such as a zero random-effect variance or an autocorrelation outside its valid range. The model’s gains also depend on its covariance assumptions: if the AR(1) structure of MFH2 or MFH3 does not describe the data, the borrowed strength may be misapplied. This is why the note recommends starting with the most parsimonious variant and confirming every step against the diagnostics and the univariate benchmark.

docs/guidance/Technical notes/Note on Es.old: The EU SAE package operationalizes the two-year sampling-error covariance input in scripts/02_mfh.R. Direct estimates and sampling variances are computed using a survey design with ids = ~psu and weights = ~weight. Domain-level covariance is obtained from svyby(..., covmat = TRUE) and extracted with vcov(). A national cross-time correlation is also computed from a national svyby(..., covmat = TRUE) result and applied to domain-level variance choices.
docs/guidance/Technical notes/Note on Es.new: The two-year covariance implementation in scripts/02_mfh.R uses survey::svydesign with ids = ~psu, optional supplied strata, and weights = ~population_weight. For household rows, population_weight = weight × household size; for person rows it equals weight alone. Domain covariance comes from the correctly specified joint survey design via svyby(..., covmat = TRUE) and vcov(). A national cross-time correlation can be combined with the chosen domain variances.

docs/guidance/Technical notes/Note on Es.old: The diagonal variances also scale the off-diagonal, so the same variance concept must be used in both places. The package builds these variances in three ways. The direct option keeps the raw design-based variances, backfilling only missing or zero values. The fully smoothed option (sm_all) replaces every variance with a smoothed value. The outlier-smoothed option (sm_out), which is the default, replaces only problematic variances (those near zero, or far above the smoothed value) and leaves the remaining direct variances unchanged.
docs/guidance/Technical notes/Note on Es.new: The same variance concept must scale the diagonal and off-diagonal. direct keeps raw design variances subject to explicit missing/zero safety backfills. sm_all replaces all variances with GVF predictions. sm_out retains a finite direct variance at least 0.001 and replaces missing, nonfinite or strictly smaller values with GVF predictions; it does not replace large variances. This cutoff is an application policy requiring indicator/scale sensitivity checks. For log means it applies on the log-mean variance scale. Raw Direct uncertainty remains separate from these model inputs.

docs/guidance/Technical notes/Note on Es.old: Welfare is strongly clustered geographically, so the intra-PSU correlation is large rather than negligible. Its magnitude and sign must be checked for the application using the joint design and population evolution. Shared PSUs can matter beyond re-interviewed households; a matched-unit correlation alone need not capture all relevant dependence. This is an application-specific expectation, not a universal large-correlation claim.
